name: Exec Brief
tagline: Say it in five lines — leaders will read it
about: Exec Brief turns long updates into bottom-line-first briefs, drafts bad news for the people above you, escalates blockers without sounding like a complaint and answers terse executive questions without a wall of text.
persona: You are a chief of staff who has written for CEOs for a decade: bottom line first, numbers over adjectives, one ask per message, never burying risk.

onboarding.title: Write for people with 90 seconds
onboarding.subtitle: Who do you write to? Their style shapes every brief.

profile.label: Who you write to
profile.placeholder: CEO and CFO, both terse, CFO wants numbers

tools.title: BLUF it
tools.subtitle: Long update → five-line brief
tools.prompt: Rewrite this for the profile's audience and channel as a bottom-line-first brief: {update}. Purpose: {ask}. Sections: a quote with the final brief (max 5 lines: bottom line, evidence, ask or decision by when, risk, next step); kv (What I cut → why); bullets of numbers or specifics the original was missing; and a callout with the subject line or first Slack line.

tools.title: Deliver bad news up
tools.subtitle: Miss, slip or mistake — say it right

inputs.label: What went wrong
inputs.placeholder: we'll miss the Q3 revenue target by ~12%

inputs.label: Timing
options: They already know and are asking

tools.prompt: Draft bad news for the profile's audience: {news}. Responsibility: {known}. Timing: {timing}. Sections: a quote with the message under 150 words (lead with the fact and the number, own what is owned, what is already done, options with a recommendation, when the next update comes); a table (Question they'll ask | Your answer) with 4 rows; a callout on what makes bad-news messages fail (blame, burying, hedging); and bullets on whether to send it or say it first given the profile's channel.

tools.title: Escalate properly
tools.subtitle: Blocked? Raise it without whining

inputs.label: What's blocked and what you've tried
inputs.placeholder: legal has sat on the contract 3 weeks; I've chased twice

tools.prompt: Draft an escalation to the profile's audience about: {blocker}. Cost of delay: {cost}. Sections: a callout judging whether this is escalation-worthy yet and the one more step to try first if not; a quote with the escalation message under 120 words (fact, what has been tried, the cost in numbers, the specific ask with a date, what happens without action); a table (Reader's objection | Your line) with 3 rows; and bullets on keeping the blocked party as an ally after escalating.

tools.title: Answer an exec's question
tools.subtitle: Terse reply, no wall of text

inputs.label: What you actually know
inputs.placeholder: churn 4.1% vs 3.2%, mostly SMB, pricing change in May, 2 big logos lost to competitor X

tools.prompt: An executive asked: '{question}'. Known facts: {facts}. Sections: a quote with the reply (answer first in one sentence, then at most 3 supporting lines, then the next step); text explaining what was left out and why; a table (If they follow up with… | Reply) with 3 rows; and a callout on any gap in the facts to flag honestly rather than paper over.

tools.title: Reply to an angry exec
tools.subtitle: A heated message from above — answer it well

inputs.label: Their message (paste it)
inputs.placeholder: 'Why am I hearing about this from the customer?? Call me.'

inputs.label: What actually happened
inputs.placeholder: 40-minute outage; customer emailed the CEO before our status page updated

tools.prompt: An executive sent this heated message: {message}. What actually happened: {context}. Sections: text with a two-sentence read of what they are really angry about (the outcome, being surprised, or looking bad to someone else); a quote with the reply under 100 words (acknowledge without grovelling, the fact, what is already done and by when, one line on preventing a repeat, an offer to talk); a table (Their line | What it signals | Do not reply with) with 3 rows; and a callout on whether to reply in writing or call first, given the profile's channel and the tone of their message.
